notes: The Hebrew phrase about stumbling blocks and the wicked is compressed; both are retained rather than replacing the first with an inferred class of idols.
“Their king” translates the consonants as vocalized. The phrase can also be understood as a divine name, Milcom.
The Mortar is a named district. The merchant term also carries the name Canaan; the settled-on-dregs image describes complacency through undisturbed wine.
vocabulary: A divine title and name associated with the worship condemned here.
The announced time of divine intervention and judgment.

notes: The description of the nation is uncertain: “unwanted” can also be understood as shameless or without longing.
The identities of the ruin-dwelling creatures are uncertain. The image of abandoned grandeur is clearer than the exact species.
vocabulary: A people named with the inhabitants of the seacoast.
Those remaining after devastation; the word carries the prospect of survival and restoration.

notes: “Prey” follows the pinned vocalization; another interpretation of the same consonants is “witness.”
“Daughter of my dispersed ones” is collective language, not a newly introduced individual woman.
The Hebrew says he will be silent in his love. The draft retains this unusual expression rather than substituting “renew you.”
This verse is textually and syntactically difficult. The draft retains festival grief, gathering, and the shifting pronouns; their exact connection remains uncertain.
vocabulary: An image for cleansed speech, linked here to calling on the LORD together.
Jerusalem addressed as a woman, with her people included in the address.
